paragraphs.text: Lesson 6. The perfect puppy. Will is trying to buy a dog, and Susan is helping him at the pet shop.
First, listen to their conversation and try to answer the comprehension questions.
Gee, I don't know. I really wasn't looking for a dog that size. My kid is seven years old. I'm not sure he can handle a big dog.
A German Shepherd is a very good dog. They're smart and loyal and very protective. Also, this one's still a puppy and not a full grown adult yet.
Your son and the German Shepherd can grow up together.
Yeah, that's true. But the problem is I live in a very close-knit residential neighborhood. Eventually, the German Shepherd will get bigger and big dogs bark.
Even if my son could handle a dog that size, I'm not sure my neighborhood could.
Okay, I understand your concerns. So let's narrow it down to small dogs. How about, say, a St. Bernard?
What?
I was just pulling your leg.
Gee, you scared me.
Listen, please, all I want is a little puppy. Maybe a chihuahua?
Nah, guys aren't chihuahua-type people, especially seven-year-old. Kids have lots of energy. Your son needs a puppy that can keep up with him.
You know, run around, play fetch and whatnot.
Oh great, just what I need. Two tornadoes running loose in my house. Why did my son have to ask for a puppy for his birthday?
Why not a turtle or a lizard or a fish?
Calm down, Dad. We'll find the right puppy.
Besides, turtles are boring, fish poop too much, and lizards aren't exactly cuddly.
Okay, what other kinds of puppies do you have?
I was thinking a Dalmatian.
Still too big, and I've heard they're aggressive. If he bit one of the neighbors, they'd sue me.
Okay, so forget the Dalmatian. How about a pug? They're small and full of energy.
Nah, they're ugly and their eyes give me the creeps.
You're not making this easy.
I'm sorry, but the puppy has to be just right. Don't get me wrong, I love big dogs.
I had a Georgia bloodhound when I was a kid. Great dog. But the fact is that my neighbors whine if the leaves fall off the trees too loudly.
That's why I live on a farm. No neighbors within ten miles. Okay, let me think.
I'm all ears.
Hey, I got it. How about a toy fox terrier? They're small, playful, full of energy, and very affectionate.
Hey, yeah, I think that's just my work. Do you have any here?
A mother just gave birth to a litter of four. The puppies aren't weaned yet, but they should be by the time your son's birthday arrives.
Terrific. Yeah, a terrier is just right.
Is there anything else I can help you with? Do you want to buy a feeding dish, a collar, maybe some dog toys?
Not yet. I want to bring my son with me so he can pick them out. But there is one more thing. My wife wants a bird. Not too big and not too small.
Here we go again.
Here are some vocabulary words that will help you understand the dialogue better.
Will is looking for a puppy for his son. The word puppy means a baby dog. We also have a specific word for a baby cat. A baby cat is called a kitten.
Will doesn't want a big dog because he lives in a very close-knit suburban neighborhood.
The word close-knit describes a community where the people have close relationships.
Will is concerned that the German shepherd will get bigger and big dogs bark. The word bark is a verb. It refers to the sound a dog makes.
Susan says she understands his concerns. Then she says, so let's narrow it down to small dogs.
The phrasal verb narrow down means to reduce the number of options.
Susan suggests a st. Bernard, but that's also a big dog. When Will is surprised, Susan says, I was just pulling your leg.
Pulling your leg is an idiomatic expression. It means joking or not being serious. Another way to say this is, I was just kidding.
Will suggests a chihuahua, but Susan rejects that idea because she says your son needs a puppy that can keep up with him.
Keep up with him means accompany him at the same speed. Some of the activities that Will's son might want to do with his dog are run around and play fetch.
Play fetch refers to a game when you throw a ball or a stick for the dog to get and bring back to you. That's called playing fetch.
Will responds, oh great, just what I need. Will is using the phrase, oh great sarcastically. He doesn't think it's great. He actually thinks it's bad to have two tornadoes running loose in my house.
Running loose means running without limits or restraint. In other words, Will doesn't want both his son and the dog running around in his house and probably causing a lot of destruction.
Will wishes that his son had asked for a different animal like a turtle, lizard or fish, but Susan says that turtles are boring, fish poop too much and lizards aren't exactly cuddly.
The word cuddly means able to be hugged and held in the arms with affection. Cuddly is the adjective form. The verb for holding something in your arms and squeezing it with affection is cuddle.
Next Susan suggests a dalmatian, but Will says that's still too big and he's heard that dalmatians are aggressive. Will says, if he bit one of the neighbors, they'd sue me.

The word sue is a verb meaning to bring legal action against someone. Then Susan suggests a pug saying they're small and full of energy, but Will says, nah, they're ugly and their eyes give me the creeps.

The expression give me the creeps means it makes me afraid or repulsed. Will says the puppy has to be just right. Don't get me wrong. I love big dogs. This phrase, don't get me wrong means don't misunderstand me.
Will is using this to clarify his opinion about big dogs. However, he says, the fact is that my neighbors whine if the leaves fall off the trees too loudly.
The word whine means complain often in an immature way. Susan says, okay, let me think and Will responds, I'm all ears. This expression, I'm all ears means I'm listening eagerly and carefully.
Then Susan says, hey, I got it. We use this phrase, I got it. To say, I have an idea or I've solved the problem.
Susan suggests getting a toy fox terrier and Will likes this idea. He asks, do you have any here? And Susan responds, a mother just gave birth to a litter of four.
When a dog or cat gives birth to a group of babies, the group of babies is called a litter. Susan then says the puppies aren't weaned yet.
Weaned means trained to stop needing the mother's milk. At the end of the dialogue, Susan asks if Will wants to buy anything else, like a feeding dish or a collar.
A collar is a strip of fabric or plastic that goes around the dog's neck. Collars can be used to identify a dog or to connect the collar to a leash.
A leash is a long strip or cord. You hold the other end of the leash in your hand to make sure the dog stays close to you.
Will doesn't want to buy anything yet. He says, I want to bring my son with me so he can pick them out.
This phrasal verb, pick them out, means choose them. But Will also wants to buy a bird for his wife, not too big and not too small.
Then Susan says, here we go again, meaning that the same situation or a similar situation or in this case dialogue is probably going to be repeated.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation. Go ahead and try the vocabulary quiz to put these expressions into practice and the speaking task to get some feedback on your spoken English.
